description: Junctional beats, nodal escape, accelerated nodal rhythm, and JET

questions.stem: Premature junctional contractions (PJCs) are characterized by:

options.text: Delta wave and short PR interval
Wide QRS complex with compensatory pause
Narrow QRS without preceding P wave, or with retrograde P wave (inverted in II, III, aVF)

questions.explanation: PJCs arise from the AV junction, so they activate the ventricles normally (narrow QRS). The P wave may be: 1) Absent (buried in QRS), 2) Before QRS with short PR (<120ms), or 3) After QRS (retrograde). Retrograde P waves are inverted in inferior leads because atria activate from bottom to top.
questions.clinical_pearl: P wave location in junctional rhythms depends on relative speeds of antegrade (to ventricles) and retrograde (to atria) conduction. If retrograde is faster, P appears before QRS. If slower, P appears after QRS.

questions.stem: A healthy 10-year-old has occasional narrow complex beats without preceding P waves on Holter monitor. The child is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassurance - isolated PJCs are usually benign

questions.explanation: Isolated PJCs in structurally normal hearts are benign and require no treatment. Like PACs and PVCs, occasional junctional ectopy is common and clinically insignificant in asymptomatic children with normal hearts.
questions.clinical_pearl: Benign ectopy: PACs, PJCs, and isolated PVCs in structurally normal hearts generally don't require treatment unless frequent (>10-20% burden), symptomatic, or causing cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with acute myocarditis has a heart rate of 85 bpm with narrow QRS and no visible P waves. What is the most likely rhythm?
questions.explanation: The narrow QRS at 85 bpm without P waves indicates a junctional rhythm. The rate (60-120 bpm) makes it 'accelerated' rather than escape or tachycardic. Myocarditis can cause enhanced junctional automaticity. This is usually self-limited as the inflammation resolves.
questions.clinical_pearl: Accelerated junctional rhythm causes: Digoxin toxicity, Myocarditis, Post-cardiac surgery, Hypoxia/ischemia. Usually resolves with treatment of underlying condition.

questions.stem: Junctional ectopic tachycardia (JET) is characterized by:

options.text: Narrow complex tachycardia (120-260 bpm) with AV dissociation and retrograde atrial capture
Wide complex tachycardia with AV dissociation
Irregular narrow complex tachycardia with fibrillatory baseline

questions.explanation: JET features: 1) Narrow QRS (junctional origin), 2) Very fast rate (120-260 bpm in post-op, slower in congenital), 3) AV dissociation (atrial rate slower than ventricular), 4) Occasional retrograde capture of atria. The ventricular rate exceeds atrial rate - opposite of typical SVT!
questions.clinical_pearl: JET diagnostic clue: Ventricular rate > Atrial rate with narrow QRS. In most tachycardias, atrial and ventricular rates are equal or atrial is faster. JET is the exception!
